extracted.intended_audience: power plant developers, regulated entities, EPA rulemaking stakeholders, and regulators (participants in EPA's NSPS/BSER rulemaking on CCS for new natural gas-fired combined cycle EGUs)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evidentiary criteria the EPA uses to determine that carbon capture and sequestration (CCS) is an adequately demonstrated Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) for new natural gas-fired combined cycle (NGCC) electric generating units.

rubrics_metrics.name: 90 percent CO2 capture achievable
rubrics_metrics.description: A 90 percent CO2 capture standard is achievable for natural gas-fired combined cycle combustion turbines and is the capture rate relied on for the BSER determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA concludes that 90 percent capture is achievable over long periods (i.e., 12-month rolling averages) for base load combustion turbines based on project examples, demonstrations, and analyses. Numerous announced commercial and EPAct05-assisted projects targeting at least 90–95 percent capture are cited as supporting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cross-technology evidence (coal-fired CCS supports NGCC CCS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence from CCS on coal-fired steam generating units supports the adequacy of demonstration for CCS on combined cycle EGUs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA relies in part on the demonstration and learnings from coal-fired CCS projects (e.g., Boundary Dam Unit 3) while noting differences (coal impurities vs. natural gas). This cross-technology evidence is used to corroborate that 90 percent capture is achievable for NGCC units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with range of flue gas conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: CCS must operate effectively across the range of post-combustion flue gas conditions expected from NGCC units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA notes NGCC post-combustion flue gas is relatively uniform with low impurities; small differences (e.g., NOx) are manageable, particularly if installed with SCR. Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) can increase CO2 concentration and reduce O2 and flow rate, aiding capture. The Agency concludes that small differences would not adversely impact capture equipment operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational flexibility: turndown and load-following capability
rubrics_metrics.description: CO2 capture systems must be compatible with normal NGCC operational variability including turndown and load-following.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single trains of capture facilities have turndown capabilities of ~50 percent; two-train arrangements can effectively turndown to ~25 percent throughput. Capture rates have been shown to be higher at lower throughputs. Strategies such as producing and holding additional lean solvent during off-peak hours can ensure capture performance during variable load operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Startup and shutdown do not preclude high capture rates
rubrics_metrics.description: CCS must be able to achieve high capture efficiencies during cold/hot startups and shutdowns without limiting the combustion turbine operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA identifies process strategies (reserve lean solvent, dedicated heat storage for reboiler preheating, fast starting steam cycle technologies or high-pressure bypass extraction) modeled to show 95 percent capture rates can be achieved during startup. Cold startups typically take ≤3 hours and shutdowns <1 hour; natural gas post-combustion flue gas does not require coal-like pretreatment, enabling earlier capture during startup.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPAct05-assisted projects as corroborative (not sole) evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Projects that received EPAct05 assistance may be used to corroborate but cannot be the sole basis for an adequacy-of-demonstration determination under EPA's interpretation of EPAct05.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA may rely on EPAct05-assisted projects to support or corroborate other information but identifies a subset of underlying non-EPAct05 evidence (e.g., coal-fired unit demonstrations, Net Power information) as sufficient by itself to support the 90 percent capture determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: CO2 pipeline transport is adequately demonstrated
rubrics_metrics.description: Pipeline transport of captured CO2 is an adequately demonstrated component of CCS for newly constructed or reconstructed NGCC units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA relies on the history of CO2 pipeline build-out, expanding network of trunklines, recent new pipelines, EPAct05-assisted pipeline examples, and comprehensive PHMSA regulation of supercritical CO2 pipelines. Co-location with storage sites (minimizing transport) is also an option. CO2 captured from NGCC compressed and delivered into pipelines is indistinguishable from CO2 from coal-fired units, so prior evidence applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geologic sequestration (storage) is adequately demonstrated
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-term containment of CO2 in subsurface geologic formations is adequately demonstrated as part of CCS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA points to numerous injection projects, widespread availability of deep saline formations/unmineable coal seams/depleted oil & gas reservoirs, and a regulatory framework (UIC Class VI under SDWA, GHGRP under CAA). EPA experience in permitting, state primacy for Class VI, and improvements to permitting processes support the determination. DOE/USGS data show extensive national sequestration potential and geographic availability analyses indicate most of the U.S. is within 100 km of suitable formations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Siting flexibility and options to serve load without nearby sequestration
rubrics_metrics.description: If a geologic sequestration site is not within an area, project developers can either build pipelines to remote storage or site the EGU near storage and transmit electricity to load areas ('gas-by-wire').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA describes two developer options: (1) locate near load and transport CO2 via pipeline to storage, or (2) site closer to geologic sequestration and deliver electricity via transmission. Historical precedents ('coal-by-wire') and existing transmission infrastructure (RTO/ISO planning, long-distance supply examples) support gas-by-wire feasibility. EPA's geographic availability memorandum assesses these tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost reasonableness of CCS for new combined cycle units
rubrics_metrics.description: The costs of installing and operating CCS (capture, transport, and storage) for new combined cycle units are considered reasonable relative to other control costs and BSER factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA evaluated capture, transport, and storage costs and compared them to other control costs deemed cost-reasonable in prior rulemakings. The analysis accounts for reductions due to the IRC section 45Q tax credit and other federal incentives. EPA concludes the costs are reasonable based on NETL and other analyses and projected cost declines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture cost metrics and technical drivers
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific quantified cost and performance impacts from installing a 90 percent capture amine-based post-combustion system on a new combined cycle EGU are used as evaluative metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NETL (Oct 2022) estimates: capital costs increase ~115% ($/kW), heat rate increases ~13%, incremental operating costs increase ~35%, and unit derates ~11%. For base load combustion turbines, LCOE increases by ~62% (about $27/MWh) and estimated onsite CO2 reduction cost ~$81/ton ($89/metric ton) pre-45Q. Technical drivers include lower CO2 concentration (≈one-third of coal), larger volumetric flow per MW, higher O2 concentration (≈3x coal), and absence of coal impurities. EGR can mitigate some drivers by increasing CO2 concentration and reducing flow/O2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR) as a cost/performance strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of EGR/FGR is a viable process strategy to improve flue gas conditions for capture and reduce costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One study cited found EGR can decrease capital costs by 6.4%, decrease heat rate by 2.5%, decrease LCOE by 3.4%, and decrease overall CO2 capture costs by 11% relative to a combined cycle EGU without EGR. NETL cost estimates used by EPA do not assume EGR, so EGR represents a plausible avenue for cost reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected cost declines from learning, R&D, and policy support
rubrics_metrics.description: Projected reductions in capture, transport, and sequestration costs over time due to technological progress, scaling, learning rates, and public policy support (DOE funding, IIJA, IRA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA cites historical learning rates (5–27% reductions per doubling), studies projecting capture+compression costs falling from ~$95/ton (circa 2015) to ~$50/ton by 2025, target project pricing (~$40/ton), and Nth-of-a-Kind illustrative capital cost reductions (~25%). DOE funding programs, OCED Carbon Capture Demonstration Projects, and IIJA/IRA policies are expected to accelerate cost declines by reducing capital costs, uncertainty, and supply-chain maturation.

rubrics_metrics.name: CO2 transport and sequestration cost estimation guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Use standardized modelling/guidelines for estimating pipeline transport and sequestration costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NETL's 'Quality Guidelines for Energy System Studies; Carbon Dioxide Transport and Sequestration Costs in NETL Studies' and the CO2 Transport Cost Model are cited as sources for estimating pipeline capital, related capital expenditures, and O&M costs, as well as sequestration cost estimates.
